lens: Adversarial audit for silent failures — code that returns a plausible number where it should return an error or a null. I read the measurement engine, the leak detector, the trial counter, the benchmark constructors and the two completed studies, then ran the actual pipeline against the parquet archive and reproduced the published headline result before attacking it. The headline claim under audit is research/studies/filing_categories.md: "order wins beat the benchmark 63.2% vs a 43.3% random baseline, z = +13.4". I reproduced it (62.7% vs 43.3%) and then took it apart.

findings.problem: The event sampler is documented as "sampled evenly across time, not truncated", but when `found` is between 1x and 2x `max_events` the integer division gives `step = 1`, so `.iloc[::1].head(2500)` is a pure head-truncation of a date-ordered frame. Because `find_events` returns `ORDER BY a.trade_date`, the study keeps only the OLDEST events. The random baseline is built separately and spans the whole period, so the signal cohort and the comparison cohort cover different calendar windows.
findings.evidence:
Ran the shipped sampler for every category (start=2022-01-01, max_events=2500):

category        found step   kept  date span kept            true span
expansion        1870    1   1870  2022-01-03 -> 2026-09-07  2022-01-03 -> 2026-09-07
orders           4086    1   2500  2022-01-03 -> 2024-01-12  2022-01-03 -> 2026-09-07
guidance        49781   19   2500  2022-01-03 -> 2024-09-04  2022-01-03 -> 2026-09-07
ratings          3243    1   2500  2022-01-03 -> 2024-06-07  2022-01-03 -> 2026-09-07
results         15793    6   2500  2022-01-03 -> 2024-08-12  2022-01-03 -> 2026-09-07
mna              8003    3   2500  2022-01-03 -> 2024-08-28  2022-01-03 -> 2026-09-07
capital          7700    3   2500  2022-01-03 -> 2024-10-17  2022-01-03 -> 2026-09-07
volume_query     2246    1   2246  2022-01-03 -> 2026-09-07  2022-01-03 -> 2026-09-07

Baseline dates by year: {2022: 9, 2023: 9, 2024: 9, 2025: 9, 2026: 4}
Orders event dates by year: {2022: 1259, 2023: 1160, 2024: 81}

Re-running measure/summarise four ways (12-month horizon, beat-benchmark %):
  ORDERS as-shipped (2022-01..2024-01)      62.7%   median stock +35.3%   complete 2500/2500
  ORDERS random 2500 over the full span     53.3%   median stock +14.4%   complete 2439/2492
  BASELINE as-shipped (2022..2026)          43.3%   median stock  +6.1%   complete 1983/2400
  BASELINE date-matched to shipped orders   50.5%   median stock +22.7%   complete 2400/2400

Published edge: 63.2 - 43.3 = +19.9pp. Like-for-like (untruncated orders vs full-span baseline): 53.3 - 43.3 = +10.0pp. Date-matched the other way: 62.7 - 50.5 = +12.2pp. Median excess falls from +15.9% to +3.9%. At 24m: published +15.3pp becomes +10.4pp date-matched.

The published table's own ordering is the tell: the only two categories NOT truncated (expansion 53.4%, volume_query 47.0%) are the two worst performers.
findings.why_it_inflates: The kept events sit inside the 2022-2023 Indian small/mid-cap melt-up while the baseline is spread evenly to 2026, including 2025-2026 entries with much weaker forward returns. Roughly HALF of the headline 20-point edge is calendar composition, not signal. The study's caveats section says "the comparison is relative and the relative gap is real" — that sentence is false as run. The signal does survive at about half the claimed size.
findings.fix: Replace `.iloc[::step].head(n)` with a sampler that cannot truncate — e.g. `ev.sample(n, random_state=...)` or stratified sampling within calendar month — and, separately, build the random baseline from the *sampled event dates themselves* rather than from an independent even grid, so signal and baseline are date-matched by construction. Also assert in `main()` that `kept.signal_date.max()` is within a few weeks of `ev.signal_date.max()` and fail loudly if not. The same line exists at jobs/study_volume.py:119 (step=55 there, so that study escaped it by luck, not by design).

findings.line_hint: line 24 — "z = +13.4 against the baseline on n = 2,379"
findings.problem: The significance statement treats every filing event as an independent observation. It is not: the 2,500 events come from 701 symbols across 25 calendar months, with 12- and 24-month holding windows that overlap almost completely, in one market regime. 72% of the events are repeat appearances of a symbol already in the sample. No clustering correction appears anywhere in zen/validation/, and `trials.deflated_sharpe` (which does correct for search) is never called by either study.
findings.evidence:
On the as-shipped orders sample at 12m:
  p = 0.627, n = 2500, distinct symbols = 701, distinct months = 25
  symbols with >1 event = 415; 72% of events are repeats of an already-present symbol
  NAIVE binomial z vs 0.433:            +19.6
  month-clustered bootstrap SE of p:    0.0176 vs naive SE 0.0097  (SE understated 1.8x)
  clustered z vs 0.433:                 +11.0
  clustered z vs date-matched 0.505:    +6.9
findings.why_it_inflates: An understated standard error makes the result look unfalsifiable ('not ambiguous'), which is precisely the frame that stops anyone re-checking it. Combined with finding #1 the real z is +6.9, not +13.4 — still significant, but no longer beyond question, and small enough that the next confound could erase it.
findings.fix: Compute the beat-rate standard error by clustering on calendar month (or on a block bootstrap over non-overlapping 12-month blocks) and on symbol, and report the clustered z. Add the clustered-bootstrap helper to zen/validation/trials.py next to deflated_sharpe, and make summarise() emit distinct-symbol and distinct-month counts alongside `scored` so that a sample of 2,500 events over 701 names can never again be reported as n = 2,500.

findings.line_hint: 98-103 — `def value(shares, prices)` and its comprehension guard
findings.problem: The docstring says "ignoring names that stopped trading -- a delisted holding is worth its last price, not nothing, and assuming zero would understate the benchmark." The code does the opposite of what the comment claims: a held name with no price row that day is simply omitted from the sum, so it contributes zero to the portfolio value. Every rebalance then rebases the capital on that depressed level, locking the loss in permanently. Nothing errors; the level just comes out low.
findings.evidence:
On average 0.124% of held names have no price row on any given session (median 0.086%, p95 0.381%, max 0.89%). Running portfolio_index over 2016-01-01..2026-09-07 as shipped versus an identical run that carries the last known price forward (what the docstring describes):
  as-shipped (missing name = worth 0):      2070.9  ->  +7.05%/yr
  carry-forward last price (documented):    2713.0  ->  +9.79%/yr
  understated by 31.0% cumulative, 2.74pp per year
The module docstring's headline figure — "Over 2015-2026 it returned about 2.2x, roughly 7% a year. This is the honest hurdle for a stock-picking strategy" — is the buggy number.
findings.why_it_inflates: The stated hurdle for 'did picking beat not picking' is 2.74pp/yr too low. Any strategy judged against `broad` gets a free ~2.7 points a year. This is the same failure mode as the 1.9-million benchmark the docstring boasts about having fixed — a benchmark artefact that flatters everything measured against it — and the fix comment now describes behaviour the code does not have.
findings.fix: Maintain a `last_price` dict updated each session and mark held shares to `prices.get(s)` if present else `last_price[s]`, which is what the docstring already promises. Add a regression assertion that the broad index level never falls more than the equal-weighted median constituent return on any session — a name vanishing from the panel should be invisible in the level. Note this module is currently dead code (eventstudy uses the `indices` Nifty 500 table), so fix it before anything imports it.

findings.line_hint: 55 and 66 — the docstring claim and `AND p.turnover >= {min_turnover_cr * 1e7}`
findings.problem: The event set is filtered on the turnover of the trade_date session — the very session the filing lands on. The docstring asserts "The liquidity join uses the session the filing lands on, which is known at that point -- it does not look ahead." It is not known at the filing moment, and more importantly the filing itself is a cause of that day's turnover. The screen therefore selects filings that already produced a market reaction, and silently discards filings in thin names that nobody noticed.
findings.evidence:
Median signal-day turnover, orders events vs the baseline's eligible universe on its own dates:
  ORDERS events           median 19.75 cr  (n = 2500)
  BASELINE universe       median 10.55 cr  (n = 50874)
The event stocks trade at roughly double the baseline universe's turnover on the selection day — an abnormal-volume tilt introduced by the filter, not by the category.
findings.why_it_inflates: It is selection on a post-signal outcome. The retained events are the ones the market already reacted to, and post-attention drift is a known effect that has nothing to do with 'a contracted future cash flow from a named counterparty'. It also breaks the symmetry with the random baseline, whose 1-crore floor is a plain liquidity screen rather than a reaction screen.
findings.fix: Filter on liquidity measured strictly BEFORE the filing — e.g. median turnover over the 21 sessions ending the day before trade_date — and require the same pre-event window in `es.baseline`. Then re-run: if the orders edge is a reaction effect it will shrink again. Correct the docstring either way.

findings.line_hint: 202-220 — the `elif delisted:` branch and the `bm_ret` block below it
findings.problem: For a delisted name the stock is exited at its last traded price and marked `complete=True` at every horizon, but the benchmark leg is still measured to the full horizon target date. Stock return and benchmark return are therefore computed over different windows, in a function whose docstring promises "The index return is measured over the identical calendar window as the stock, from the same entry date." No null, no warning — just an excess_return that mixes a 2-month stock leg with a 24-month index leg.
findings.evidence: Orders sample, 24-month horizon: 92 rows flagged delisted. Actual days held: median 374, p10 = 51. 25 of the 92 were held under 180 days yet are scored as 24-month outcomes against a full 730-day benchmark leg. Separately, at 12m over a 4,000-event volume sample, 516 of 3,999 events (12.9%) were flagged delisted, and 25 benchmark legs hit the silent `bm_exit = float(bm.iloc[-1]["close"])` fallback at line 218 — which shortens the benchmark window while the stock keeps a full one.
findings.why_it_inflates: Two ways. The `bm.iloc[-1]` fallback truncates only the benchmark leg, so the stock is credited with return over a window the index is not — a direct inflation of excess_return. And the delisting asymmetry corrupts the study's own 'order-filing companies delist less' argument (90 vs 134 in the write-up), since those counts come from cohorts covering different calendar spans (date-matched, the baseline shows 186 delisted, not 134).
findings.fix: For a delisted name, measure the benchmark over the SAME truncated window (entry -> sym_last), not to `target`. Where the benchmark series genuinely runs out before the stock's exit, return None rather than falling back to `bm.iloc[-1]` — an incomplete benchmark is a null, not a shorter window. Add a `holding_days` column to Outcome so a 51-day 'two-year' result is visible in the output.

findings.line_hint: 46 (`SELECT * FROM prices WHERE date <= ?`) and 78 (`passed = full == truncated`)
findings.problem: Two holes in the harness the whole project rests on. (1) `_truncated_copy` copies only the `prices` table — `store.SCHEMA` defines nothing else — so the truncated archive has no announcements, financials, indices or corpactions. The filings work now driving the project cannot be leak-tested at all. (2) `future_blindness` reports `passed: True` when the strategy emits zero signals both times, so a strategy that silently returns [] (which `Momentum.generate` does on four separate early-return paths) certifies as future-blind.
findings.evidence:
tables in truncated archive: ['prices']
querying announcements in truncated archive -> CatalogException: Table with name announcements does not exist!

future_blindness on a strategy whose generate() returns []:
{'test': 'future_blindness', 'strategy': 'emits_nothing', 'asof': date(2020,1,1), 'passed': True, 'signals_full': 0, 'signals_truncated': 0}
findings.why_it_inflates: A green leak report is the thing that licenses trusting every downstream number. A vacuous pass, or a whole data source the detector structurally cannot see, means the guarantee is narrower than it reads — and the announcement pipeline is exactly where the next one-day-shift bug would live. tests/test_leak.py asserts `signals_full > 0` for momentum, but `stability()` and every other caller do not.
findings.fix: Have `_truncated_copy` truncate every table present in the source archive (prices on `date`, announcements on `an_dt` — not trade_date — financials on the filing timestamp, indices and corpactions on their date columns), driven off `SHOW TABLES` rather than a hardcoded prices schema. And make `future_blindness` raise, or at minimum set `passed=False`, when `signals_full == 0`: a strategy that says nothing has not been tested.

findings.problem: The stock leg runs from the entry session's OPEN; the benchmark leg runs from that same session's CLOSE. The two windows differ by one session's intraday move, contradicting the module docstring's BENCHMARK ALIGNMENT paragraph.
findings.evidence: Mean entry-day open->close return across 3,999 volume-spike events: -0.68% (median -0.86%). That whole amount sits in the stock leg and in none of the benchmark leg. Sign and size are signal-dependent — here it deflates, for a signal with positive day-after drift it would inflate by a comparable margin.
findings.why_it_inflates: A systematic ~0.7pp offset per event, applied to every horizon, on the same order as the median excess returns the studies are trying to resolve (+3.9% for the corrected orders result).
findings.fix: Use the index's own `open` on the entry date for `bm_entry` — the indices table already carries an `open` column (verified: date, index_name, open, high, low, close, points_change, pct_change, volume, turnover). One-line change, and it makes the docstring true.

findings.problem: Category order and pattern breadth put the wrong filings in the buckets the studies then test. `\border(s|ed|ing)?\b` matches 'SEBI order', 'NCLT order', 'adjudication order', and `orders` is evaluated BEFORE `litigation`, so regulatory actions are scored as order wins. `guidance` is evaluated before `ratings` and its `outlook` / `investor meet` terms swallow almost the entire investor-relations calendar. Nothing errors; the buckets just are not what their names say.
findings.evidence:
Of 5,392 filings categorised 'orders':
  1,120 (20.8%) match sebi order|nclt|court order|tribunal|adjudicat|show cause|penalt
  only 1,867 (34.6%) match anything resembling a genuine win (letter of award/intent, work order, purchase order, bagged, order from...)
Of 58,959 filings categorised 'guidance':
  58,084 (98.5%) are investor-presentation / analyst-meet / conference-call scheduling and transcript notices
  104 mention 'outlook' at all
Sample 'guidance' subjects are all of the form 'Schedule of Analysts/Institutional Investor Meet', 'Transcript', 'Investor Presentation'.
Also: 13% of the 'routine' bucket is matched only via the attachment body, not the description — real news can be binned as routine because its PDF text mentions a newspaper publication.
findings.why_it_inflates: The published table's row labels misdescribe what was measured. 'Guidance / investor update, 50.9%' is really 'a company scheduled an analyst call' — a proxy for being a covered, actively-followed name, which is a size/attention factor, not news. And a fifth of the headline 'order wins' bucket is regulatory trouble, meaning the genuine-win subset's edge is being measured through 21% opposite-signed noise.
findings.fix: Move `litigation` above `orders`; anchor the orders pattern to win language (`letter of (award|intent)|work order|purchase order|bagg|secur(es|ed) .{0,20}order|receipt of .{0,20}order`) rather than the bare word 'order'; move `ratings` above `guidance` and drop bare `outlook` from guidance; rename the bucket to `ir_event` since that is what it holds. Then re-run the study — the labels are what the write-up reasons from.

findings.line_hint: ~178 — `entry_px = float(entry["adj_open"] or entry["adj_close"])` and the two guards below it
findings.problem: A NaN adjusted open defeats all three defences. `float('nan') or x` returns nan because nan is truthy, then `if not entry_px` is False and `entry_px <= 0` is False, so the nan flows through to `stock_return`. Because it is nan rather than None, the `stock_ret is not None` test at the Outcome construction also passes.
findings.evidence: Confirmed by construction: `float('nan') or 5.0` -> nan; `not float('nan')` -> False; `float('nan') <= 0` -> False. Zero occurrences in the 4,000-event volume sample and the 2,500-event orders sample (the archive currently has no NaN opens on entry sessions), so this is latent rather than active.
findings.why_it_inflates: It does not today. It is on the list because it is a silent-failure shape rather than an error: the three guards read as belt-and-braces and none of them fires, so the day a NaN open appears the rows disappear from `scored` in summarise() with no count and no warning.
findings.fix: Replace with an explicit check: `o = entry["adj_open"]; entry_px = float(o) if pd.notna(o) and o > 0 else float(entry["adj_close"])`, then `if not np.isfinite(entry_px) or entry_px <= 0: skipped += 1; continue`. And have measure() return/log a count of skipped events — right now events dropped for any reason (no price series, no session after the signal, bad entry price) vanish silently.

findings.problem: Delisting is detected relative to the maximum date among the STUDY'S OWN symbols, not the archive's last session, because `adjusted_prices` was called with `symbols=` restricted to the event set. For a narrow study the reference point moves with the sample.
findings.evidence: For the 1,724-symbol volume sample the subset max equals the archive max (2026-09-07), so the current studies are unaffected. But by construction, a single-symbol study of a delisted name gives `last_session == sym_last`, so `delisted` is False, the horizon runs past the data, and the outcome is dropped as incomplete.
findings.why_it_inflates: It reintroduces exactly the survivorship bias the module docstring exists to eliminate, and it does so only for small or focused samples — the ones most likely to be run ad hoc on a promising idea. A delisted loser silently becomes an 'incomplete window' instead of a bad outcome.
findings.fix: Query the archive's true last session once (`SELECT max(date) FROM prices`) and use that as the delisting reference, independent of which symbols the study asked for.

findings.problem: When the subject line does not match `_SPLIT` or `_BONUS`, the action is recorded with `factor = None` and `adjustment_factors` then filters it out with `factor IS NOT NULL`. The corporate action is known to exist and is silently left unadjusted.
findings.evidence: corpactions holds 408 splits and 448 bonuses; 14 splits and 11 bonuses (25 in total, 2.9%) have a NULL factor and are therefore invisible to the price adjustment. Every other action type is NULL by design (15,086 dividends, 9,627 'other', 284 rights).
findings.why_it_inflates: It does not inflate — an unadjusted split reads as an 80% crash, which drags the affected names down. It is here because it is a silent hole in the very correction the module docstring calls out as biasing 'exactly the stocks a momentum or quality screen would pick', and because 25 unexplained -80% outcomes in a study of a few thousand events is enough to move a median.
findings.fix: Log a warning listing the unparsed subjects at load time, and have `adjustment_factors` surface a count of dropped split/bonus rows so a study can see how many of its names are knowingly unadjusted. The 25 subjects are few enough to widen the regex or hand-map.

findings.problem: trade_date rolls Saturday and Sunday forward but knows nothing about exchange holidays, and the 15:30 boundary uses `minute > 30` so a filing stamped 15:30:00-15:30:59 (after the close) is attributed to the same session. Downstream, `study_filings.find_events` inner-joins prices on `p.date = a.trade_date`, so any filing landed on a holiday matches no price row and drops out of the study without a count.
findings.evidence: Code inspection plus the join at jobs/study_filings.py:64-65. The archive has 2,671 index sessions across 2015-11..2026-09 against ~2,830 weekdays, so roughly 6% of weekdays are holidays; filings rolled onto one are silently unrecoverable.
findings.why_it_inflates: Sample attrition that is not random — it concentrates on the days after long weekends and festival closures, and it is invisible because the join produces fewer rows rather than an error.
findings.fix: Roll trade_date forward to the next date present in the prices calendar rather than to the next weekday, and change the boundary test to `an_dt.time() >= time(15, 30)`. Have find_events report `found` alongside the count of filings that failed the price join.
